data.name: The Spectrum Retreat
data.detailed_description:
Faz Check-in no The Spectrum Retreat para uma estadia inesquecível. Manipula o teu caminho para a verdade neste emocionante jogo de puzzles com narrativa.



O Spectrum Retreat é um desafiante jogo de puzzle na primeira pessoa jogado num futuro próximo. Acordas no hotel The Penrose, um pacífico mas perturbador refúgio do mundo exterior. Sendo um estimado hóspede, a tua existência está embebida nos corredores e nos quartos de hóspedes do The Penrose.

A exploração do fantástico hotel estilo art-déco irá desvendar os mistérios do The Penrose e das incertezas que envolvem a tua estadia. Contudo, teu desejo de descobrir a verdade é obstruído por uma série de puzzles com códigos de cores, desafios com leis da física que dão a volta à cabeça, e o medo cada vez maior das tuas verdadeiras intenções serem reveladas.

reviews.review:
I went into this game with fairly held back expectations given that the reviews I was being shown at the time were a little mixed. This game is a bit unusual, but I can confidently say that I enjoyed it.

Although the game advertises itself as a narrative first-person puzzle game, I think it would actually be more accurate to describe it as half walking simulator, half first-person puzzle game. 
If you go into this hoping for a pure puzzler, I could see why you would be a bit disappointed. Honestly, I played this game when I was a little bit braindead but for whatever reason still wanted to play a puzzle game. I ended up really appreciating the walking sim sections that happen between the portal-esque puzzler sections. It gave my weary 2 brain cells a little rest before I had to fire them back up again, so it was a format I actually enjoyed. 
Usually with first-person puzzle games that want to run a narrative at the same time, the game will drip-feed you dialogue between puzzles, or even sometimes just talk through the puzzles. That format needs balance, as sometimes (especially when these games ramp up in difficulty) you get half a conversation point and need to solve the puzzle before you get the other half. With my ADHD I’ve already wondered off 3 times, got distracted and completely forgot what they were talking about by the time they finish their point after I’ve finished the puzzle so sometimes to me it’s just unnecessary stop-starting that makes me less invested in the narrative. With this game, there is absolutely no talking or anything during the puzzling parts. I could just lock in and do the puzzles and then come back out already in “Okay I’m listening” mode. The game incorporates this format into the story, so it didn’t feel out of place in my opinion.

The walking sim sections were fun, the only criticism I have for those parts are that when you’re given something to do the game gives you audio hints way too quickly. At one point it told me to do something, I instantly knew what it wanted me to do and it genuinely gave me a hint before my brain had signalled my body to press the keyboard button to move my character in the direction I knew I had to go. I really wish there was a way to toggle these hints on or off in the options as they were just really not necessary. Other than that I found these sections engaging and at times kind of creepy! This wasn’t something that I was expecting, I honestly don’t play a lot of horror-esque games so it was putting me on edge because frankly, I’m a baby. I’m sure hardened horror players will think it’s nothing, but it managed to make me jump once and I definitely felt relieved to get into the puzzle areas a few times because it was making me uncomfortable!

As for the puzzle sections, I enjoyed these too, with maybe a few caveats.
Going back and looking at the trailer, I notice that the trailer for the game is actually a little vague on how the puzzles work. You essentially have a device that can “absorb” a colour. This can let you pass barriers of that colour, and there are multiple colours, so you need to use this colour-swapping mechanic to navigate obstacles. The first few puzzle areas use the same kind of puzzles, and by the end of that second section I was already feeling that if the puzzles carried on like that, it would be quite a slog to get through. Thankfully though, just as it was starting to get a little tiresome the game switches up the puzzle types and then keeps it interesting from there. It was a slow start, but definitely stick it out and it gets better. I went from feeling like the puzzles were bordering boring to being really engaged in some of the puzzles and enjoying some of the newer concepts it introduces as you go along.
Another caveat worth mentioning is that this game is not afraid to force you to reset the puzzle. This didn’t bother me, as I seemed to be in the mood to not mind trial & error and I didn’t feel like the puzzles were necessarily long or tedious enough to annoy me having to reset, but it’s definitely something you’ll need a little patience for. Some newer games in this genre have implemented a rewind feature, and I think this game would have been a good candidate for that as well.

When it comes to the story I thought this was kind of a cool concept and did find it enjoyable slowly figuring out what was going on (even if parts were fairly predictable to me). The game has a surreal aspect to it, which I always enjoy in games. You’re in a hotel and all of the staff are mannequins with assumingly AI personalities. This within itself is quite creepy, but I noticed early on that in your room you can cross the day off of the calendar. At the next opportunity to interact with the calendar, your character crosses off the same day.
At first I found the voice-acting a little weird, and unnatural. This was until you’re contacted in game by a character. This character is so much more natural sounding, and more, I guess, human. From there I actually thought the voice acting was pretty decent, as the contrast of the human character makes the voice-acting of the AI staff feel intentional. I think that main voice-actor did a great job. Admittedly, after a while I noticed that there is kind of a lot of loud breaths and mouth noises from this woman which was a little uncomfortable… but overall for an indie game it’s decent. The music was quite nice as well, which is always a bonus.

Something I wasn’t expecting from this game was a little bit of philosophical thinking. The game doesn’t outright encourage you to think of these things, It is not a clear and defined theme of the game and I can’t really go into it without essentially spoiling the game, [Spoiler]but an interesting question arises that if a past version of a person made a decision, and the present version hasn’t the capacity to remember that decision, should that decision be upheld? Are those two people even still the same? To muddy the waters here as well, how is this affected when the decision is made around bad behaviour? If a person no longer remembers what they did, are they still liable for punishment, or is it immoral to punish someone who has no recollection of their actions? To an extent it reminded me of a Black Mirror episode that was questioning this same thing.[/spoiler]
It was interesting to think about the story a little and ask myself those questions. The plot itself didn’t feel water-tight, it felt like there were some plot holes here and there so it wasn’t 100% satisfying and probably could have used a little bit more refining, but I enjoyed it nonetheless and like the concept.

Overall, the game felt like it was made well and I found it interesting, enjoyed the concept and the format.
It’s also a fairly easy one to 100% although requires a second playthrough. I did it back to back as realistically once you know what you’re doing it doesn’t take that long to get through it again. [spoiler]I also very much enjoyed the Hotel California references in the achievements, as I remember finding that song very creepy when I was a kid![/spoiler]
